document.title: Issue Paper for Vice President of the United States (VPOTUS), "Counterterrorism Activities (Neo-Taliban)"
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
document.note: [Secret] Observes that some Taliban leaders operate with relative impunity in Pakistani cities and may still enjoy support from lower echelons of ISI. The insurgency (Taliban, al-Qaeda, HiG, Haqqani, Jaish-i-Muslimeen) is not monolithic. It describes Kabul's strategy and reconciliation programs (PTS with over 800 former fighters, DDR, DIAG), and notes the Taliban's increasingly lethal tactics: suicide bombing, IEDs and assassinations.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Described as using suicide bombings and IEDs and assassinating pro-government religious leaders, tribal elders and officials; recruits from Pashtun tribesmen in Afghanistan and Pakistan; leaders operate from Pakistan.

organizations.name: Al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Leaders said to provide guidance and support from Pakistan for cross-border operations.

organizations.name: Inter-Services Intelligence
organizations.notes: Lower echelons may still support Taliban leaders.

organizations.name: Hizb-i-Islami Gulbuddin
organizations.notes: Former members are reconciled through the PTS program.

organizations.name: Government of Afghanistan
organizations.notes: Runs the reconciliation program and the DDR and DIAG processes.

organizations.name: Program for Strengthening Peace
organizations.notes: Reconciles former Taliban and HIG members; about 800 former fighters had joined by December 2005.

organizations.name: Disarmament of Illegal Armed Groups
organizations.notes: Began work in June 2005; a province-by-province effort to disband the most notorious illegal armed groups.

organizations.name: Taliban Peace and Reconciliation Program
organizations.notes: A partnership to decide which former Taliban can be reintegrated into Afghan society. The document calls it moderately effective.

organizations.name: al-Qa'ida
organizations.notes: Named as a threat the GOA aims to eliminate.

events.description: Volume of violence in Afghanistan rose; Taliban shifted to more suicide bombings and IEDs and assassinations of pro-government clerics, elders and officials.

Issue paper for the Vice President drafted on counterterrorism activities (Neo-Taliban).

Mr. Hadley asked a (redacted) GOA official to clarify the GOA strategy for eliminating the Al-Qaeda and Taliban threat in the next two to three years. The answer: military action first, then the Taliban reconciliation process, then improved relations and security cooperation with Pakistan.

key_claims: Taliban violence increased in 2005, with more suicide bombings, IEDs and assassinations of pro-government figures.
Taliban and al-Qaeda leaders provide guidance and support for cross-border operations from Pakistan.
Some Taliban leaders operate with relative impunity in Pakistani cities and may still receive support from lower echelons of the ISI.
The Taliban recruits fighters from its Pashtun tribal base in Afghanistan and Pakistan.
The Afghan reconciliation program (PTS) is moderately effective but has not yet realized its potential, with about 800 fighters enrolled by December 2005.
The Afghan Government strategy rests on military action, Taliban reconciliation, and improved relations and security cooperation with Pakistan.

The GOA strategy for eliminating the al-Qaeda and Taliban threat rests first on military action, second on the Taliban reconciliation process, and third on improving relations and security cooperation with Pakistan.
The Afghan government's reconciliation program for lower and mid-level Taliban fighters was assessed as moderately effective but not yet at its potential.
The GOA supports reconciliation and restoration with former Taliban where possible.
The U.S. supports the reconciliation program and the decisions taken by the GOA.
